lawyer: M Hafizullah with SK Siddique and Md Al-Amin Sarker, Advocates — For the Petitioner.
parties:
Black Sea Shipping Company (Blasco) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Continental Traders  ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
2. The opposite party filed execution case being Title Execution Case No. 1 of 1997 under section 44A CPC on the basis of a judgment passed by a High Court of Justice, Queen''s Bench Division, Commercial Court UK against the judgment debtor. By an order dated 14-7-97 the learned Judge ordered for attachment of the vessel MV SOKOL now berthed at Chittagong Port, Chittagong. The petitioner thereafter filed an application under section 13(b) and 44A read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the execution case and also filed an application for vacating the order of attachment dated 14-7-97. In the aforesaid application it is stated that the decree-holder did not file the certified copy of the judgment and decree in the execution case and the judgment was passed ex parte as such the same is not conclusive and the execution case is not maintainable. Furthermore the judgment was not passed on merit. It has also been stated in the aforesaid application that no summons was issued upon the defendant-petitioner and the Court had no jurisdiction to pass such decree. In that view of the matter the execution case is liable to be rejected and the vessel is liable to be released from attachment forthwith. 

 3. The opposite party decree-holder had filed a reply to the application for rejection of the execution case and stated that the allegations of the petitioner are not at all correct. It is stated that summons were issued twice. First of all on 8-1-96 and then on 14-8-96. The defendant after receiving the writ amended the points of claim but they did not appear as such under the law in UK. The default judgment was passed on merit of the case after considering the points of claim and therefore it does not fall within the scope of section 13(b) CPC. As to the jurisdiction it is stated that Continental Traders and Black Sea Shipping Company by an agreement signed between them submitted themselves to the jurisdiction of English Court and the law prevailing. It also shows that the Court has jurisdiction to execute the said foreign judgment. Section 44A CPC reads as follows: 

 "44A—(1) Where a certified copy of decree of any of the superior Courts of the United Kingdom or any reciprocating territory has been filed in a District Court, the decree may be executed in Bangladesh as if it has been passed by the District Court. 

 (2) Together with the certificated copy of the decree shall be filed a certificate from such superior Court stating the extent, if any, to which the decree has been satisfied or adjusted and such certificate shall, for the purpose of proceedings under this section, be conclusive proof of the extent of such satisfaction or adjustment. 

 (3) The provisions of section 47 shall as from the filing of the certified copy of the decree apply to the proceeding of a District Court executing a decree under this section, and the District Court shall refuse execution of any such decree, if it is shown to the satisfaction Of the Court that the decree falls within any of the exceptions specified in clauses (a) to (f) of section 13. 

 Explanation 3—"Decree", with reference to a superior Court, means any decree or judgment of such Court under which a sum of money is payable, not being a sum payable in respect of taxes or other charges of a like nature or in respect of a fine or other penalty." 

 4. Mr M Hafizullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, argues vehemently that section 44A CPC lays down the law that a certificated copy of a decree of any of the superior Courts of the United Kingdom or any reciprocating territory is to be filed. Together with the certified copy of the decree shall be filed a certificate from such superior Court stating the extent to which the decree has been satisfied or adjusted. It is stated in this application that no certified copy has been filed before the Executing Court. Only a photocopy of the same has been filed which cannot satisfy the requirement of the certified copy as embodied in section 44A CPC. The learned Additional District Judge has held that the copy can very well be treated as certified copy because it bears the seal and signature of the Court concerned. Moreover, the same carried Notorial Certificate which has been authenticated by the High Commission of Bangladesh in UK. In this application photocopy of the certified copy of the Judgment is shown to have been annexed at page 30 of this petition but it appears that only the first page has been annexed and the remaining pages are totally absent. The petitioner ought to have annexed the judgment as a whole. This sort of practice we do not approve. The point raised before the learned Additional District Judge that the requirement of section 44A CPC having not been complied with strictly the learned Additional District Judge ought to have rejected the execution case in terms of section 13(b) CPC. Section 13 CPC reads as follows: 

 5. Mr M Hafizullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the impugned judgment has not been pronounced by a Court of competent jurisdiction. He has further submitted that the judgment has not been passed on merit of the case. The learned Additional District Judge in his judgment has observed that the District Judge has authority to proceed with the execution case under section 44A CPC and that the decree-holder Continental Traders and the judgment-debtor Black Sea Shipping Company (petitioner) by signing an agreement submitted themselves to the jurisdiction of English Court and the learned Judge also referred to the Article 12 of the agreement in support of the jurisdiction. The learned Judge observed that the judgment was passed upon following the Supreme Court Rules in UK and on the face of the judgment and procedure the learned Judge continued to hold that the case has been decided on merit. Therefore the exceptions as enumerated in section 13 CPC do not attract the present case as the judgment was pronounced by the Court of competent jurisdiction and the same has been passed on merit although the defendant did not appear. Section 44A sub-section (3) provides that the provision of section 47 shall apply and the District Court shall refuse execution of any such decree, if it is shown to the satisfaction of the Court that the decree falls within any of the exceptions specified in clauses (a) to (f) of section 13 but section 47 CPC has been omitted by Ordinance No. XLVIII of 1983 as such the aforesaid section 47 is not at all applicable as enumerated in section 44A CPC. Therefore sub-section (3) of section 44A requiring that a decree falls within the purview of clauses (a) to (f) of section 13 the executing Court will refuse to execute such decree does not arise. 

 6. As to the attachment of the ship in question the executing court has already passed the order for sale of ship MV SOKOL. Since the executing Court is invested with the power to execute the decree the order passed is well within full jurisdiction. The learned Additional District Judge appears to have committed an error of law in passing the impugned order, as such, the aforesaid order does not call for any interference by this Court.
